## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ with Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ and simple quotients $D^{\mu}$ in the signed conjugate normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), together with the dominance order on partitions of $n$ ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]).

[F1] ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) $S^{\lambda}=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ and $D^{\mu}=(D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ for the conjugate partitions, where $S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}$ is the Murphy cell module and $\theta$ is the involutive automorphism $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$; pullback along $\theta$ is exact and preserves submodules, quotients, composition multiplicities and simplicity.

[F2] ([[cor-cellular-decomposition-matrices-are-dominance-unitriangular]]) For the Murphy cellular basis of $H$ the composition multiplicity $[S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]$ satisfies $[S^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ whenever $D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$ and is zero unless $\nu\unrhd\rho$.

[F3] ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) Conjugation reverses dominance: $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ if and only if $\mu\unrhd\lambda$.

[F4] ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]) $D^{\mu}\ne0$ exactly for the $e$-regular $\mu$.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Invariance of composition multiplicities under the normalisation: by [F1] the twist $(-)^\theta$ is an exact equivalence of module categories with inverse $(-)^\theta$ itself, so it is additive on short exact sequences and carries composition series to composition series; hence $[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}]=[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]$ for all $\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$. [given, F1, F4]

2.1 Vanishing: if $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$, then $[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]\ne0$ by step 1.1, so $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ by [F2], and conjugation reversal [F3] gives $\mu\unrhd\lambda$. [step 1.1, F2, F3]

2.2 Diagonal: taking $\lambda=\mu$ in step 1.1 gives $d_{\mu\mu}=[S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 Assembly: steps 2.1 and 2.2 are exactly the two claims; ordering the rows and columns of $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ by any linear extension of dominance displays the unitriangular shape, and no off-diagonal entry is determined by the cellular structure. At $q=1$ the statement specialises to the classical symmetric-group unitriangularity of [[thm-symmetric-group-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]] by [F4]. [step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Construct the lower-rank action directly over the given field. Put $M_0=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Lambda(n-1,r-1)}M^\alpha$ for $H(r-1)$. Length-additive parabolic coset bases give $M^{(\alpha,1)}\cong M^\alpha\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ by $x_\alpha h\otimes a\mapsto x_\alpha ha$. Thus the summands with last coordinate $1$ form $M_1\cong M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$. The functorial algebra homomorphism $f\mapsto f\otimes1$ embeds $S(n-1,r-1)$ into $\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(M_1)$: the Hecke algebra $H(r)$ is free on its parabolic coset basis and contains the unit coset, so the map is injective. Extend these maps by zero to the remaining summands of $M$ and put $p=\sum_{\alpha_n=1}1_\alpha$. For every left $S(n,r)$-module $V$, $V^1=pV$ is therefore a natural $S(n-1,r-1)$-module. This supplies the lower-rank action without assuming that the first level is a sum of root-adjacent highest-weight spaces, and without adjoining a square root of the Hecke parameter. It agrees with the last-coordinate polynomial level of [F3]. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 Prove the Hom assertion algebraically. For $S=S(n,r)$ put $\overline W=Se\otimes_{eSe}eW$ and let $\varepsilon:\overline W\to W$ send $se\otimes w$ to $sw$. Its image is $SeW=W^{(e)}$, which is $W$ under the stated hypothesis. Applying $e$ identifies $e\varepsilon$ with the isomorphism $eSe\otimes_{eSe}eW\to eW$. Exactness of $e(-)$ therefore gives $eK=0$ for $K=\ker\varepsilon$. The exact sequence is $$0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow\overline W   \xrightarrow{\varepsilon}W\longrightarrow0.$$ For any $S$-map $g:\overline W\to V$, its image $g(K)$ is an $S$-submodule killed by $e$, so it is contained in $V_{(e)}=0$. Thus $g$ factors uniquely through $W$. The adjunction then gives $\operatorname{Hom}_H(eW,eV)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(\overline W,V) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(W,V)$. This proves assertion 2, with the kernel and quotient in the correct direction. [given, F1]

2.1 Reconcile the corners for all $n\ge r$. Put $\omega_*=(1^{r-1},0^{n-r},1)$ and $e_*=1_{\omega_*}$. Both $M^\omega$ and $M^{\omega_*}$ are the regular module $H(r)$. Their fixed identity isomorphism gives block matrix units $u,v\in S(n,r)$ with $u=e_*ue$, $v=eve_*$, $uv=e_*$ and $vu=e$. Thus multiplication by $u$ gives a natural isomorphism $eV\to e_*V$, with inverse multiplication by $v$, and carries the standard regular corner action to the $e_*$ corner action. When $n=r$ these corners coincide. This explicitly supplies the natural corner identification instead of treating an idempotent with last coordinate $0$ as lying in the first level. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 Construct a perfect Schur-contravariant form on the permutation-summand module $M$. On each distinguished coset basis $b_d=x_\alpha T_d$, put $\beta_\alpha(b_d,b_c)=\delta_{dc}q^{\ell(d)}$. The row generator cases are a same-row scalar $q$, or an adjacent length-increasing pair with $b_dT_i=b_c$ and $b_cT_i=q b_d+(q-1)b_c$, $\ell(c)=\ell(d)+1$. Their weighted diagonal matrices verify $\beta_\alpha(aT_i,b)=\beta_\alpha(a,bT_i)$, so the forms are Hecke-contravariant and perfect. To prove Schur adjointness, work first in $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$. Length-additive cosets and [F4] give $\tau(a^*b)=P_\alpha(Q)\beta_\alpha(a,b)$ on $M_\alpha$, where $P_\alpha=\sum_{u\in S_\alpha}Q^{\ell(u)}$ is nonzero in $A$ with constant coefficient $1$. For $f=\varphi_{ST}:M_\nu\to M_\mu$, $a=x_\nu h$ and $b=x_\mu k$, membership in [F4] gives $m_{TS}x_\mu=P_\mu m_{TS}$ and $x_\nu m_{TS}=P_\nu m_{TS}$. Thus $$P_\mu\beta_\mu(fa,b)=\tau(h^*m_{TS}x_\mu k)=P_\mu\tau(h^*m_{TS}k),\qquad P_\nu\beta_\nu(a,f^*b)=\tau(h^*x_\nu m_{TS}k)=P_\nu\tau(h^*m_{TS}k).$$ Cancel the nonzero polynomials only in $A$, then specialize the resulting identity to $F$. It identifies the left $S$-module $M$ with $M^\circ$. No Poincare factor is canceled in the given field, including at $q=1$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Compute the first-level corner inside this induced action. The lower regular summand is $H(r-1)$, whose induction is $H(r-1)\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)=H(r)$, exactly the summand of type $\omega_*$. The lower corner operator given by left multiplication by $h\in H(r-1)$ induces left multiplication by the same $h$ on $H(r)$ under $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$. Thus every generator $T_1,\ldots,T_{r-2}$ acts exactly as its image in the upper regular corner, by equality of these explicit endomorphisms. This is an algebra-level calculation; it needs no generic semisimplicity or cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 Determine the simple socle labels of $M$. Evaluation at $1$ in the regular summand gives $Se=\operatorname{Hom}_H(H,M)\cong M$ as a left $S$-module. Finite-dimensional star duality and [F4], together with step 2.2, give $$\operatorname{Hom}_S(L,M)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(M^\circ,L^\circ)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(Se,L)\cong eL$$ for every simple $L$. Thus every simple submodule of $M$ has restricted label; for restricted $\lambda$, any nonzero map $L(\lambda)\to M$ is injective. 4.1 Transfer composition multiplicities by exactness, not by a Hom-space count. Apply $f_{n-1,r-1}$ to a finite composition series of $L_n(\lambda)^1$. Step 3.1 identifies its result with $\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}$, proving the stated equality. Assertion 3 is not used to claim that every composition factor survives; a socle statement alone would not justify that claim. [F2, step 3.1]

4.2 Prove the restricted-socle assertion over every original field. Applying $p$ to the injection $L_n(\lambda)\to M$ of step 3.2 embeds $L_n(\lambda)^1$ into $pM=M_1=M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ with the actual lower action of step 1.1. Sign restricts along the group tower, is exact, and preserves the two compared multiplicities. This is the ordinary group interpretation, including characteristic $2$; it is not an untwisted identification of a restricted label with the same regular label. Steps 3.1, 1.2, 4.2 and 4.1 prove all the assertions. [F5, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 4.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, a unit $q$, the type-A Hecke algebra $H$, its additive Jucys-Murphy elements $L_k$ and its Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with basis $(m_t)$.

[F1] The standard basis multiplication, the quadratic and braid relations, and the integral row action are those of [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]. In particular $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$, and $x_\rho T_i=q x_\rho$ if $i,i+1$ lie in one row of $t^\rho$.

[F2] The integral Murphy basis, dominance ideals, cell multiplication and finite Garnir straightening are proved in [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]. We write $I^{\rhd\lambda}=H^{\rhd\lambda}$ and $x_\lambda=m_\lambda$. The proof there supplies the dominance support rule: if $s'=ss_i$ is standard with $s\rhd s'$ and $\ell(d(s'))=\ell(d(s))+1$, multiplying any same-shape term strictly above $s$ by $T_i$ and then straightening produces only standard terms strictly above $s'$. Straightening a nonstandard row-standard tableau only raises its tableau order in the same shape. All these identities hold over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ and specialize along $v\mapsto q$.

[F3] A finite-dimensional algebra has nilpotent Jacobson radical and semisimple quotient ([[thm-jacobson-radical-is-nilpotent-and-the-quotient-is-semisimple]]). ## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, a unit $q$, the type-A Hecke algebra $H$, its Murphy cells $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and form quotients $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$, and the ordinary signed-conjugate normalization in the Statement.

[F1] The nonzero cell-form quotients are pairwise distinct absolutely simple modules and exhaust the simples. A quotient is nonzero precisely when its form is not identically zero; a zero form quotient makes no assertion about the actual module head ([[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]).

[F2] The actual ordinary module/form bridge gives $S^\lambda=C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ and $D^\lambda=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$, with $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i$ an involution commuting with star. Pullback is exact and preserves nonzero modules and simplicity ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Conjugation exchanges regular and restricted partitions ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).

[F3] The locally proved Jucys–Murphy elements commute and preserve a common tableau flag of each Murphy cell, with diagonal word $([c_t(1)]_q,\ldots,[c_t(n)]_q)$, where $c_t(a)$ is the integer node content. The row-filled maximal tableau has an exact eigenrelation ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

[F4] Cellular support gives $[C_{\mathrm M}(\eta):D_{\mathrm M}(\rho)]=0$ unless $\eta\unrhd\rho$, and gives diagonal multiplicity one when that quotient is nonzero ([[cor-cellular-decomposition-matrices-are-dominance-unitriangular]]).

[F5] The integral Murphy basis, dominance ideals, row action and finite Garnir straightening are valid over $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$ and commute with every base change ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). For a row group $S_\alpha$, $x_\alpha^2=[\alpha]!_Qx_\alpha$ by length-additive parabolic cosets; $[\alpha]!_Q=\prod_j[\alpha_j]!_Q$ ([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]).

[F6] At $q=1$, the quantum characteristic is the field characteristic when positive, and is infinity in characteristic zero ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); the ordinary group labels are the regular Specht-head labels ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). The Jacobson radical of a finite-dimensional algebra is the intersection of the annihilators of its simple modules ([[def-jacobson-radical-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Use finite joint-primary projections without presupposing which labels survive. The regular right module has a cellular filtration with quotients copies of the cells; refining their common flags in [F3] gives a simultaneous triangular flag on it. Thus each $L_a$ is annihilated by a polynomial $\prod_b(X-b)^N$, with finitely many diagonal values $b\in F$ and $N\ge\dim H$. Polynomial Bezout and the Chinese remainder construction give $p_{a,b}$ congruent to one modulo $(X-b)^N$ and zero modulo the other factors. Substituting $L_a$ gives commuting idempotents. For a joint word $\xi$, their product $P_\xi$ is idempotent in $H$ and on a cell flag has diagonal one exactly at tableaux with word $\xi$, zero elsewhere. An idempotent has zero image if and only if all these diagonal entries vanish: its triangular matrix would otherwise be nilpotent and idempotent, hence zero. The vector-space functor $M\mapsto MP_\xi$ is exact on $H$-modules, because a lift $x$ of $y=yP_\xi$ can be replaced by $xP_\xi$, and kernels are preserved. No centrality or $H$-submodule assertion for this image is needed. [F3, F5, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For finite $e$, equality of two diagonal values $[a]_q,[b]_q$ is equivalent to $a\equiv b\pmod e$. Indeed $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ for all integers, including negative integers. When $q\ne1$, $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$, and when $q=1$, $e=\operatorname{char}F$ and the q-integer is the integer reduced to $F$. Thus a joint word is exactly a residue word in the node convention $c-r\pmod e$. [given, F3, F6, algebra]

1.3 Prove the complete ladder-boundary comparison. Put $L(s,c)=(e-1)s+c-e$. Suppose $\alpha$ is restricted, every occupied node has $L<l$, and the addable ladder-$l$ set is nonempty. Set $C=l+e-1$, $T=\lfloor C/(e-1)\rfloor$, $d=C-(e-1)T\in\{0,\ldots,e-2\}$ and $u_s=C-(e-1)s$. For $1\le s\le T$, $0\le\alpha_s\le u_s$, and no positive row occurs beyond $T$. The deficits $h_s=u_s-\alpha_s$ are nonnegative and satisfy $h_{s+1}-h_s=\alpha_s-\alpha_{s+1}-(e-1)\le0$. An addable ladder-$l$ row has deficit zero; thereafter every deficit is zero. Consecutive such rows have width difference $e-1>0$, so the ladder addables form a terminal interval $s_0,\ldots,T$. A first equality row that is not addable simply precedes this interval. Adding its bottommost $k$ nodes therefore adds in rows $T-k+1,\ldots,T$. The length of $\alpha$ is $T$ for $d>0$ and $T-1$ for $d=0$, including the empty case $T=1,d=0$. If $\beta\unrhd\alpha$ has the same size, its length is at most that of $\alpha$, by the prefix inequality at that length. For $d=0$ all addable rows of $\beta$ are at most $T$. For $d>0$ the sole possible extra row is $T+1$, with residue $-T$, different from $i=l\bmod e=d+1-T\bmod e$ since $1\le d+1<e$. Hence every addable $i$-node of $\beta$ lies in a row at most $T$. If $\gamma$ adds any $k$ of these initial addables, at row cutoff $r$ its prefix increment is at least $\max(0,k-\max(T-r,0))$, exactly the increment for the bottommost-$k$ extension $\delta$ of $\alpha$. Adding $\beta$'s prefix inequalities proves $\gamma\unrhd\delta$. This holds for every $k$ simultaneously and needs no same-content premise. [given, construct, algebra]

1.4 Prove the converse on actual Gram entries. Work in the universal Laurent domain $A$ and write $x_\eta=x_{B_1}\cdots x_{B_k}$ for the symmetrizers of the consecutive row-label intervals. For a row-standard tableau $t$, multiply $x_\eta T_{d(t)}$ successively by these symmetrizers and straighten modulo $I^{\rhd\eta}$. The row calculation is as follows. Once rows before $j$ agree with $t^\eta$, let $\beta_s$ count the labels of $B_j$ in row $s\ge j$; $\sum\beta_s=\eta_j$. Sort these labels in row-reading order to obtain $u$, so $t=uw$ with $w\in S_{B_j}$ and additive length. Therefore multiplication by $x_{B_j}$ first contributes $Q^{\ell(w)}$. The row-parabolic intersection on these labels is $S_{\beta_j}\times\cdots\times S_{\beta_k}$. Expanding its length-additive cosets gives the further factor $[\beta]!_Q$: each common intersection permutation contributes its inversion weight. After removing this intersection, the remaining sum belongs to the two-sided row ideal for the composition $(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_{j-1},\eta_j,\eta_j-\beta_j,\ldots,\eta_k-\beta_k)$, with zero parts omitted. This is the finite row-double-coset calculation in [F5], using no factorial inversion. If its sorted partition does not lie below $\eta$, its intersection with $I^{\unrhd\eta}$ has only strictly higher shapes and this term vanishes in the cell. Otherwise its prefix inequality at $j+1$ gives $\beta_j\ge\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}$ (the first $j-1$ parts are unchanged, and sorting can only increase the indicated prefix). Straightening retains the now fixed first $j$ canonical rows: maximal prefix counts on those rows cannot be raised further. This proves the same row calculation inductively for every $j$. All coefficients remain in $A$. [F5, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For restricted $\eta$, number its nodes by increasing $L$, taking lower rows first on a tie, to obtain $t_\eta$. Moving right increases $L$ by one and moving down by $e-1$, so it is standard. The diagrams $\alpha_l$ of nodes with $L<l$ and $\delta_l$ with $L\le l$ are restricted: their row widths are the minimum of the restricted widths of $\eta$ and the positive part of the affine cutoff bound, each having adjacent difference at most $e-1$. A node on ladder $l$ forces every lower positive position on that ladder to be occupied, since $\eta_{s+1}\ge\eta_s-(e-1)$. Thus $\delta_l$ adds the bottommost $a_l$ ladder addables to $\alpha_l$. Any competing standard tableau with the same full residue word has, in the corresponding block, $a_l$ additions all of residue $l$. Every such node was addable before the block: adding an $i$-node creates new addable corners only of residues $i+1,i-1$, distinct from $i$ for $e\ge2$. Starting with the empty diagrams, step 1.3 inductively shows its shape dominates $\delta_l$ at every completed block, and hence its final shape dominates $\eta$. No strictly lower shape has the word of $t_\eta$, and no same-shape tableau uniqueness is asserted. [step 1.3, construct, algebra]

3.1 Choose $P_\xi$ for the word of $t_\eta$. It has nonzero image on $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and zero image on every $C_{\mathrm M}(\rho)$ with $\rho\lhd\eta$, by steps 1.2 and 2.1. Therefore it has zero image on their form quotients. Apply the exact projection to a composition series of $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$. Some constituent has nonzero image; by [F1] and [F4] it is a nonzero $D_{\mathrm M}(\rho)$ with $\rho\unlhd\eta$. The exclusion forces $\rho=\eta$, proving the restricted Murphy quotient nonzero over the original field. This is a joint-word and cellular-support proof, not an import of cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}\ge e$ for some $j$, every surviving term at that row has $\beta_j\ge e$ by step 1.4 and is divisible by $[e]!_Q$. Later multiplication and straightening cannot remove this polynomial factor. Every Gram entry is the coefficient of $x_\eta$ in $x_\eta T_{d(s)}T_{d(t)}^*x_\eta$ modulo higher shapes; first expand its middle factor in the row-module basis and apply the proved row calculation. Thus every entry is divisible by $[e]!_Q$. Specializing $Q$ to $q$ makes that factor zero, so the entire Murphy form vanishes and $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)=0$. This concerns a common divisor of entries, not a product-of-hooks formula for a determinant. Combining with step 3.1 proves the finite-$e$ Murphy criterion. [F1, F5, step 1.4, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 For $e>n$, including infinity, distinct standard tableaux of any shapes have distinct full diagonal words. At their first unequal step the preceding diagram has size $a-1$; its distinct addable-corner contents differ by a nonzero integer of absolute value at most $a\le n$, so their q-integers differ. Induction recovers every next node. Consequently every tableau word of $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ occurs in no strictly lower cell. Exact projections as in step 3.1 and diagonal multiplicity one in [F4] show that all $\dim C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ flag factors occur in $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$; thus this quotient has the full cell dimension and its form radical is zero. In particular at $e=\infty$ every partition is restricted and has nonzero quotient. At $n=0$ the unique cell is $F$ with norm one. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Establish the complete semisimplicity clause. Put $f_\eta=\dim C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and $d_\eta=\dim D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$, with zero for a zero quotient. The Murphy basis gives $\dim H=\sum_\eta f_\eta^2$. On each nonzero quotient its nondegenerate form and the cell law supply all rank-one operators. Since the cells are right modules, their action gives a surjective algebra map $H\to\operatorname{End}_F(D_{\mathrm M}(\eta))^{\mathrm{op}}$, a full matrix algebra after transpose. Its kernels are distinct maximal two-sided ideals: equality would give the same matrix-algebra simple module, contradicting [F1]. They are pairwise comaximal. Their finite product map is surjective: for each kernel $I_a$ and each other $I_b$ choose $u_{ab}\in I_b$ congruent to one modulo $I_a$, multiply over $b\ne a$, and use these elements to isolate each prescribed matrix component. Its kernel is the radical by the complete simple list and [F6]. Hence $\dim(H/\operatorname{rad}H)=\sum_\eta d_\eta^2$. Step 4.2 makes this equal to $\dim H$ when $e>n$, giving an isomorphism with a product of full matrix algebras over $F$. When finite $e\le n$, the one-dimensional Murphy row cell has norm $[n]!_q=0$, since $x_{(n)}^2=[n]!_q x_{(n)}$. Its quotient dimension is zero while its cell dimension is one; every other $d_\eta\le f_\eta$. The dimension sum is therefore strictly smaller and $\operatorname{rad}H\ne0$. This proves both directions of part 3 without any claim that some Specht module must be reducible. [F1, F5, F6, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Apply the same exact involution to every Murphy quotient: $D^\lambda=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ is nonzero exactly when $\lambda'$ is restricted, equivalently when $\lambda$ is regular. The nonzero quotients remain pairwise distinct absolutely simple and complete by [F1] and [F2]. This proves parts 1 and 2, and step 5.1 gives part 3. At $q=1$, [F6] gives precisely the ordinary $p$-regular group classification, including characteristic two; no splitting or semisimplicity assumption was made. All selections and polynomial computations were finite, so no choice principle is used. [F1, F2, F6, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1] ∎

## Remarks

The finite ladder-boundary lemma, joint-primary projection argument and row-entry divisibility are local proofs. The cited manuscript documents their source; its erroneous displayed ladder slope and unsupported single-node truncation sentence are replaced by the complete simultaneous-block comparison above. The richest original classification and radical assertions are retained. Zero cell-form quotients are distinguished from actual module heads throughout.

[F1] Each Weyl module has simple head $L^{\lambda}$ of multiplicity one, the decomposition matrix is dominance-unitriangular, and all simple modules are obtained this way ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). In a finite-dimensional module, a simple head implies indecomposability: any nonzero direct summand has a nonzero head, so two nonzero summands would give a nonsimple head.

[F2] The corrected balanced Jantzen formula sums positive filtration **submodules**, not their successive quotients: $$\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda}_F(i)]=\sum_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],\ b<c}\bigl(\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})\bigr)[W^{\beta+h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_b-h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_c}_F].$$ Here $\beta_b=\lambda'_b+N-b$ for a fixed sufficiently long conjugate beta sequence, and the right hand symbols are alternating symbols: sort strictly decreasing, attach the sorting sign, and vanish on repeated or negative entries. The equal transfer preserves total size. Moreover $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$. This is the balanced hook-ratio formula required from [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] and [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. Its source arithmetic must be repaired before binding: the manuscript's displayed beta indices are inconsistent, while its worked Example 5.28 determines the balanced transfer.

[F3] Core-quotient and abacus theory: a weight-one partition is obtained from a packed core abacus by moving the bottom bead of one runner down one place. The bead move removes/adds a rim $e$-hook, and distinct runners give distinct partitions ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Restricted means $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i$ ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).

[F4] The exact Schur functor sends $W^{\lambda}$ to $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $L^{\lambda}$ to $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$, whose nonzero labels are precisely the restricted partitions. The ordinary Specht dictionary uses conjugation and the same $\theta$ pullback on every module ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

Each runner is packed, so replacing $x_k$ by $x_k+e$ gives precisely the $e$ weight-one partitions, denoted $\lambda_k$. For $j>k$, moving $x_j$ instead of $x_k$ gives the more dominant conjugate partition: comparing the sorted bead lists, each partial sum increases when the move starts at the larger bead. Conjugation reverses dominance, hence $\lambda_1\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. The largest original partition is $(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$, since its added horizontal first-row strip dominates every other placement. [F3, construct, algebra]

The derivative of $X^e-1$ at $q$ is $eq^{e-1}\ne0$, so $\nu([e]_X)=1$; also $\nu([h]_X)=0$ when $e\nmid h$. If $q=1$, then $\operatorname{char}F=p=e$. First work over $\mathbb F_p$ with $R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, $\hat q=1$, giving $\nu([e]_1)=\nu(p)=1$ and $\nu([h]_1)=0$ for $p\nmid h$, and then extend scalars to $F$. Consequently $i>1$ is impossible: the partition inequality $\gamma_{i-1}\ge\gamma_i+e$ would contradict this core property.
